en: The Chapter on the Bodhisattva’s Practice of the Ten Abodes, one fascicle;
translated by the Tripitaka Master Dharmarakṣa of the Western Jin.
The Bodhisattva Dharmanandita, sustained by the Buddha’s majestic spiritual power, immediately entered this [samādhi] before the Buddha.
Through the Ānupūrvaka-samādhi, one sees all the Buddhas of the ten directions—the Buddhas of the ten directions being as numerous as the dust motes in a thousand Buddha-fields;
where each single mote constitutes a Buddha-field, and such Buddha-fields extend thus throughout the ten directions and four quarters—seeing all these Buddhas of the ten directions, they all say:
"Excellent, excellent!"
“Dharmamati Bodhisattva!
The Buddhas of the ten directions all bestowed upon him wisdom and spoke to Dharmamati Bodhisattva, saying:
“It is through the merit, majestic power, and spiritual efficacy accomplished by the fundamental vows of Śākyamuni Buddha in his previous lives that you have been benefited.”
That which benefits all sutras is the benefit of the Buddha’s majestic spiritual power.
Entering deeply into the realm of the sutras, he fully reveals the dharmas of the void throughout the ten directions, with a mind free from attachment;
he enters entirely into that which is unobstructed and enters entirely into the Great Way, swiftly drawing near to the attainment of Buddhahood.
He fully knows all sutras and the thoughts of all people throughout the ten directions;
he has studied and mastered all the sutras preached in the ten directions and understands their application in every way.
For this reason, he preaches the ten stages of the bodhisattva for all bodhisattvas; having fully attained and maintained the Buddha’s majestic spiritual power, he is able to preach them all.
At that time, the discourse delivered by the Bodhisattva Dharmamati was without obstruction and without difficulty;
it was inexhaustible and without end, beyond all measure, and without limit;
none could attain its conclusion, nor could anyone determine its length.
There was never a moment of forgetfulness, nor was there anyone who did not attain clarity; all were equal and without distinction.
There was no time of indolence or arrogance, such that none could surpass him.

By the power of this samādhi, the Buddhas of the ten directions each extended their right hand and placed it upon the head of the Bodhisattva Dharmamati, causing the Bodhisattva Dharmamati to awaken within the samādhi, and then spoke to the Bodhisattva, saying:
"Listen, all you sons of the Buddha: the dwelling of a bodhisattva is exceedingly vast, as vast as empty space.

For what reason is the dwelling of a bodhisattva so exceedingly vast? Because all the Buddhas of the past were born therein; all the Buddhas of the future will be born therein; and all the Buddhas of the present are born therein."
For what reason does a bodhisattva enter the Great Way?
By what causes and conditions does one enter this Great Way?
For what reason is it exactly thus?
“Bodhisattvas have ten stages of dharma through which they discern what has been taught by the Buddhas of the past, future, and present.
What are these ten stages of dharma for bodhisattvas?”
"First is the Bodhisattva-dharma-abiding named Pāraṅgata;
second is the Bodhisattva-dharma-abiding named Ajita;
third is the Bodhisattva-dharma-abiding named Aparājita."
"Fourth is the Dharma-abiding of the Bodhisattva named Śamākī;
fifth is the Dharma-abiding of the Bodhisattva named Paryu-sapān;
sixth is the Dharma-abiding of the Bodhisattva named Ajita-sapān."
"Seventh is the Dharma-abiding of the Avaivartika Bodhisattva.
Eighth is the Dharma-abiding of the Kumārabhūta Bodhisattva."
"Ninth is the Dharma-abiding of the Bodhisattva named Yuluraja.
Tenth is the Dharma-abiding of the Bodhisattva named Avaivartika.
First, what is the Dharma-abiding of the Bodhisattva named Pāraṅgata? "

At first, he beheld the Buddha’s countenance as peerlessly upright; gazing upon his features, he could never tire of doing so. There was none who could equal him, none who could surpass him in nobility, none who could surpass him in flight, and none who could surpass him in the teachings he bestowed.

Seeing that the Buddha’s majestic spiritual power and ritual conduct were thus, this bodhisattva gradually led them into the path of the Buddha and further enlightened and guided them, teaching and delivering them all according to their individual inclinations.
Having seen those who undergo such toil and suffering, he felt compassion for them all; gradually approaching a clear understanding of the Buddha’s words, he placed his faith and inclination therein.

He newly resolved his mind to study the path of the Buddha, desiring to fully attain the Buddha’s wisdom regarding the ten difficult points, and wishing to reach a thorough knowledge of what constitutes these ten difficult points and the ten powers (*daśabala*).
“Bhāradvāja, there are ten matters taught by the Bodhisattva. What are these ten?

First, one should make offerings to the Buddhas and all bodhisattvas. Second, one should teach and speak according to what others delight in. Third, in whatever place one is born, one will always be noble and honorable. Fourth, throughout the heavens and the world, there will be none who can equal one. Fifth, all the wisdom possessed by the Buddhas shall be fully attained. Sixth, in whatever place one is born in the worlds of *parāyaṇa*, one will constantly see immeasurable Buddhas. Seventh, all profound *samādhi* sūtras shall be fully attained. Eighth, from the boundless reaches of the path of birth and death, [one shall transcend]. Ninth, once life has departed, it will not be long [before liberation]. Tenth, one shall completely deliver and liberate the people of the ten directions.”
Why is this? Because it causes one to enter further into the Buddha-dharma.
Second, what is meant by the "Dharma-abiding of the Aśvabhū Bodhisattva"?
There are ten ways of contemplating the people of the ten directions. What are these ten contemplations? First, to contemplate the goodness of all people in the world;

second, a pure and clean mind; third, a mind of universal peace and security; fourth, a supple and gentle mind; fifth, a mind of equal love for all; sixth, a mind that desires only to bestow gifts upon others; seventh, a mind that shall protect all; eighth, a mind that contemplates others as no different from one's own body; ninth, a mind that contemplates the people of the ten directions as being like teachers; and tenth, a mind that contemplates the people of the ten directions as being like Buddhas.
An Ajāśvī bodhisattva’s dharma is that he should study many sūtras;
having studied many sūtras, he should dwell in solitary seclusion;
having dwelt in solitary seclusion, he should attend upon a virtuous teacher.
Having engaged in the service of a virtuous teacher, one should remain by the side of that virtuous teacher;
having remained by the side of the virtuous teacher, one should be easy to direct;
having become easy to direct, one should act in accordance with the occasion.
Having acted in accordance with what one has undertaken, one should act with courage;
having acted with courage, one should train in entering into wisdom;
having trained in entering into wisdom, one should fully uphold all the teachings received.
Since you should fully uphold the Dharma, you should not forget it;
since you do not forget it, you should dwell in a state of peace and security. Why is this so?
"It is for the sake of benefiting and bringing compassion to the people of the ten directions.
Third, what is the Bodhisattva Dharma-abiding called *Yu-ā-shé*?
It consists of entering into all dharmas by means of ten matters."

What are these ten matters? First, all that exists is impermanent; second, all that exists is subject to suffering; third, all that exists is empty; fourth, all that exists is not "mine"; fifth, all that exists has no place of abiding; sixth, all that exists is without benefit; seventh, all that exists has no place of rest; eighth, all that exists has no location; ninth, all that exists is without attachment; tenth, all that exists is non-existent. All dharmas enter into these and do not return.
“O Āyuṣmat Bodhisattva, you should always bring to mind the people of the ten directions;
having brought to mind the people of the ten directions, you should bring to mind the spheres of the Dharma;
having brought to mind the spheres of the Dharma, you should bring to mind all the Buddha-fields.”
Having contemplated all Buddha-fields, one should contemplate the element of earth;
having contemplated the element of earth, one should contemplate the element of water;
having contemplated the element of water, one should contemplate the element of fire.
Having contemplated the dharma of fire, one should contemplate the dharma of wind;
having contemplated the dharma of wind, one should contemplate the dharma of desire;
having contemplated the dharma of desire, one should contemplate the dharma of form.
Having contemplated the phenomena of form, one should contemplate the sphere where there is no desire for the phenomena of form;
having contemplated the sphere where there is no desire for the phenomena of form, the mind has nothing to crave. Why is this?
For this reason, all should abide in the light of the Dharma.
Fourth, what is the bodhisattva’s abiding in the Dharma of *śamatha*?
There are ten matters concerning the constant mindfulness of being born in the presence of the Buddha.

What are the ten matters? First, no longer returning; second, possessing deep compassion for the Buddha; third, deeply contemplating the Dharma; fourth, regarding all people of the ten directions with a compassionate mind; fifth, contemplating that the ten directions are ultimately non-existent; sixth, that the buddha-fields of the ten directions are all empty space; seventh, that what was realized through past lives is ultimately non-existent; eighth, that all existing things are empty space, like a magical illusion; ninth, that all diligent efforts and sufferings are non-existent; and tenth, that *nirvāṇa* is empty space and non-existent.
Because of this, one is born into the Buddha-dharma; this is the teaching of the Bodhisattva Śamākī.
"The Buddhas of the past are empty and non-existent; the Buddhas of the future are empty and non-existent; the Buddhas of the present are empty and non-existent.
The Dharma of the Buddhas of the past is non-existent; the Dharma of the Buddhas of the future is non-existent; the Dharma of the Buddhas of the present is non-existent."
From what source do the mental recollections of the Buddhas of the past arise?
Upon thorough investigation, they are found to be utterly non-existent.
From what source will the mental recollections of the Buddhas of the future arise?
When sought, they are found to be utterly non-existent;
from what source, then, could the present mindfulness of the Buddhas of the ten directions arise?
When sought, it is found to be utterly non-existent.
All the dharmas of the Buddhas are fully understood to be non-existent. Why is this?
Because these dharmas of the three periods of time are all fully understood as being entirely without anything that exists.
"5. What is the Bodhisattva-dharma-abiding of *Pāyusambha*?
There are ten matters by which all the merits one has performed deliver beings throughout the ten directions.

What are these ten matters? First, to protect all people of the ten directions; second, to cause all people of the ten directions to be virtuous; third, to constantly mind the safety and well-being of all people of the ten directions; fourth, to love all people of the ten directions; fifth, to have compassion for all people of the ten directions; sixth, to instruct all people of the ten directions not to commit evil; seventh, to lead all people of the ten directions into the path of the bodhisattva; eighth, to purify all people of the ten directions; ninth, to deliver all people of the ten directions; and tenth, to liberate all people of the ten directions so that they attain parinirvāṇa.

"The people of the ten directions cannot be calculated again; the people of the ten directions cannot be numbered again; the people of the ten directions cannot be deliberated upon again; the people of the ten directions cannot be extolled again; the people of the ten directions cannot be measured again; it is utterly impossible to deliberate or speak of the people of the ten directions."
What are those who are people of the ten directions?

All people throughout the ten directions are people of emptiness; they are all not "mine"; they are all without possession; they are all that which belongs to all, and they are all without any other peculiarity.
Why is this? Because the mind has no attachments.
Sixth, what is the bodhisattva’s dharma-abiding of *ajita* (the unconquered)?
There are ten dharmas of profound compassion and pity.
What are these ten dharmas?
First, when speaking of the Buddha’s virtues or faults, the mind remains without change; second, when speaking of the Dharma’s virtues...
First, when speaking of the faults of others, his mind remains without change; second, when speaking of the virtues of others, his mind remains without change;
third, when speaking of the faults of bodhisattvas or the virtues of bodhisattvas, his mind remains without change;

fourth, when people discuss the virtues or faults of those seeking the bodhisattva path, his mind remains without change; fifth, when someone among them says that the people of the ten directions are numerous...

Sixth, regarding the few people in the ten directions, their minds have no difference; seventh, regarding all the people in the ten directions who speak of each other’s good and evil deeds, their minds have no difference;
eighth, regarding those among them who say that the people in the ten directions are easy to liberate or difficult to liberate, their minds have no difference;
ninth, regarding the teaching of the Dharma much or the teaching of the Dharma little.

The mind remains without differentiation in nine ways: ninth, whether the teaching of the Dharma is subject to destruction or the teaching of the Dharma is indestructible, the mind remains without differentiation;
tenth, whether there is a locus for phenomena or no locus for phenomena, the mind remains without differentiation.
This bodhisattva should train in these dharmas as being without location.
Furthermore, there are ten matters.
What are these ten matters?

First, all phenomena have no location; second, all phenomena cannot be found or seen as having a location; third, one studies all phenomena as being like magical transformations; fourth, all phenomena are entirely empty; fifth, all phenomena are various kinds of emptiness; sixth, all phenomena are unimpeded in the state of ultimate emptiness; seventh, all phenomena are like those produced by illusion; eighth, all phenomena are like things within a dream; ninth, all phenomena are incalculable; tenth, all phenomena are non-existent and cannot be perceived.
Why is this? Because they enter ever more deeply into the Buddha-dharma such that none can surpass them.
"Seventh, in what dharma do the *avaivartika* bodhisattvas abide?"
When a bodhisattva hears ten matters, they remain steadfastly established.
What are these ten matters?
First, whether there is a Buddha or no Buddha, they do not waver or turn back; second, whether it is said that dharmas exist or that dharmas do not exist, they do not...
First, the non-retrogression of the three [realms]; second, the non-retrogression of whether there are bodhisattvas or no bodhisattvas;
third, the non-retrogression of whether there are those who seek the bodhisattva path or no such seekers;

fourth, the non-retrogression of whether one attains this Dharma through its upholding or does not attain it through its upholding; fifth, the non-retrogression of [the presence of] various... [text truncated].
1. The Buddhas of the past; not wavering whether there are Buddhas of the past or no Buddhas of the past. 2. The Buddhas of the future;
not wavering whether there are Buddhas of the future or no Buddhas of the future. 3. The Buddhas of the present; not wavering whether there are Buddhas of the present or no Buddhas of the present.
4. The wisdom of the Buddha; [not wavering whether] the wisdom of the Buddha is exhausted or [endless].

"Without exhaustion and without returning through movement; tenth, regarding the manifold kinds of events of the past, the future, and the present, as well as those of a single kind, the mind never again moves or returns."
"This Bodhisattva should be instructed to train in these ten matters. What are the ten? First, to enter manifold wisdom from unified wisdom;

second, to enter unified wisdom from manifold wisdom; third, to enter manifold phenomena from unified wisdom; fourth, to enter unified wisdom from manifold phenomena; fifth, to sustain the people of the ten directions within empty space; sixth, to cause all of empty space to enter the people of the ten directions; seventh, to sustain mental conceptions and enter into immovability; eighth, to sustain immovability and enter into the midst of mental conceptions; ninth, to sustain empty space and enter into the midst of conceptions; tenth, to sustain conceptions and enter into empty space."
Why is this? Because all dharmas of merit enter therein; for this reason, one no longer moves.
Eighth, as for the Kumārabhūta Bodhisattva, in what dharma does he abide?
The Bodhisattva dwells in ten matters. What are these ten? First, the actions of the body, the speech of the mouth, and the thoughts of the mind are all pure and clean.

Second, there is no one who can find fault or deficiency in them. Third, with a single reflection of the mind, he knows where he will be reborn according to his desires. Fourth, he knows who among the people of the ten directions possesses a compassionate heart. Fifth, he fully knows those whom the people of the ten directions trust and rely upon. Sixth, he fully knows the various types of people in the ten directions. Seventh, he fully knows the deeds performed by the people of the ten directions. Eighth, he fully knows the formation and destruction of all buddha-fields. Ninth, through the power of supernormal travel, he reaches wherever he intends to go. Tenth, he studies the purity of all dharmas.
"This Bodhisattva should further study ten matters. What are these ten? First, one should study knowing the various Buddha-fields; second, one should study shaking the various Buddha-fields;

third, one should study the sovereign power of one's own majestic spiritual authority; fourth, one should study beholding the various Buddha-fields; fifth, one should study going from one Buddha-field to another Buddha-field; sixth, one should study traveling to incalculable Buddha-fields; seventh, one should study knowing the incalculable teachings regarding whatever is asked; eighth, one should study transformations that are like illusions and performed with sovereignty; ninth, one should study the resonance of the Buddha’s voice; tenth, one should study a single moment of mindfulness."
They reach and arrive at the places where they have made offerings to immeasurable Buddhas. Why is this?
Because by entering into a single dharma, they are sent forth to many.
"9. As for the Bodhisattva Vyūḍharāja, in what dharma does he abide?
A bodhisattva attains this through ten matters.
What are these ten matters?"

First, he fully knows all that has been produced by people throughout the ten directions; second, he fully knows all the bonds of affection held by people throughout the ten directions; third, he fully knows the origins and the ultimate ends of what people throughout the ten directions have contemplated; fourth, he fully knows the destinies toward which the past karmic roots of good and evil performed by people throughout the ten directions lead; fifth, he fully knows the various kinds of dharmas; sixth, he fully knows the various kinds of transformations contemplated by people throughout the ten directions; seventh, he fully knows the destructions and the states of good and evil within all Buddha-fields; eighth, he fully knows all matters of incalculable events in the past, future, and present; ninth, he fully knows the similarities and differences among people throughout the ten directions; tenth, he fully knows how to instruct people throughout the ten directions by preaching the Dharma of emptiness. This is it.
“Furthermore, there are ten spheres that a bodhisattva should study and understand. What are these ten spheres? First, one should study the palace of the Buddha-dharma;

second, one should study the construction of the palace of the Buddha-dharma; third, one should study all that exists within the Buddha’s palace; fourth, one should study the instructions and commands given within the Buddha’s palace; fifth, one should study the palaces from which the Buddha enters and exits; sixth, one should study the palace of the Dharma; seventh, one should study the palace of the Dharma King; eighth, one should study the instructions and commands of the Dharma; ninth, one should study the peaceful conduct of the Dharma King; tenth, one should study the acceptance and application of the instructions and commands of the newly established King of the Dharma-makers.”
Why is this? Because their minds gradually enter into the Great Way of the Buddha, and they personally apply the Dharma they have heard as instruction.
"Tenth, in what dharma does an *avaivartika* (non-regressing) bodhisattva abide?"
The Bodhisattva enters into the ten knowledges and discerns them all.
What are these ten knowledges?

First, by what cause shall I move countless Buddha-fields? Second, I shall clearly understand the affairs within countless Buddha-fields. Third, I shall daily establish Bodhisattvas within countless Buddha-fields. Fourth, I shall daily deliver the people within countless Buddha-fields. Fifth, I shall bring peace and security to the sentient beings within countless Buddha-fields. Sixth, the voices of countless people throughout the ten directions shall all hear my voice. Seventh, I shall fully know the people of the ten directions. Eighth, I shall fully know the thoughts—both good and evil—of the people in the ten directions. Ninth, I shall lead all people of the ten directions into the Buddha-way. Tenth, I shall completely deliver and liberate all people of the ten directions.

“The Bodhisattva Yulorasha cannot comprehend the conduct of the body, the speech of the mouth, the thoughts of the mind, or the actions performed by the A-vui-yan (Avinivartanīya) Bodhisattva; he is utterly unable to comprehend the affairs of the A-vui-yan Bodhisattva. He cannot comprehend the recollection of supernormal powers (*ṛddhi*), nor can he know their flight; nor can he fully comprehend the past, future, and present affairs of the A-vui-yan Bodhisattva. Furthermore, he cannot fully comprehend the Buddha-fields that the [Avinivartanīya] Bodhisattva contemplates, nor can he fully comprehend the thoughts in his mind or the actions he performs through the application of wisdom in its ten aspects.”
The Bodhisattva Yuluośa cannot comprehend the deeds performed by an Anāgāmin (A-vi-yan) Bodhisattva; this is because the Anāgāmin Bodhisattva has entered into the ten knowledges of a Buddha.
"What are the ten knowledges?
First, learning from the Buddha regarding the past, future, and present without limit or obstruction;
second, learning from the Buddha so as to fully possess all the qualities of the Buddhas; third, being without hindrance regarding the locus of all phenomena."
Learning from the Buddha: fourth, learning from the Buddha that all phenomena (*dharmas*) are without boundaries or limits and have no bottom;
fifth, learning from the Buddha that I shall protect and uphold all buddha-fields through the majestic power and spiritual authority of this merit;
sixth, learning from the Buddha that I shall clearly understand all incalculable buddha-fields and their boundless locations.
In the study of the Buddha's teachings: seventh, one should learn from the Buddha so as to bring peace and security to the infinite Buddha-fields of the ten directions;
eighth, one should learn from the Buddha regarding all the actions performed by people in the ten directions;
ninth, one should learn from the Buddha so that the wisdom of all dharmas may enter therein; tenth, one should [learn] all the wisdom possessed by the Buddha.
He knows that he has learned from the Buddha. Why is this?

Because he possesses complete knowledge and fully understands the wisdom of the Buddha; there is no longer anything further to learn from anyone else regarding the Path. This is the tenth dharma by which a Bodhisattva practices the Path in such a manner as one who has attained the state of *anavaya* (the irreversible stage).
The Sutra on the Bodhisattva’s Practice of the Path in the Ten Abodes.
